instructions:
You are reading the plain-language text of a codebase map. A reader meets each field ALONE, inside one box, with no paragraph around it, and does not read code.

Judge ONLY these two things:
  1. UNKNOWN WORD — a term the reader has not met and the field does not explain. Product words and words already in the map's Glossary are fine; jargon, an internal codename, or an unexplained abbreviation is not.
  2. LOST PRECISION — the sentence is short and plain but says nothing specific. "The system checks the user" is the shape: grammatical, readable, and it names no decision, no data and no actor. This is the worse failure, because it looks correct.

Do NOT report sentence length, em dashes, code names or an opening "It" — those are counted deterministically and the lead already has the numbers.
Be conservative. Report a field only when you can say WHICH word is unknown, or WHAT the sentence should have said. If in doubt, pass the field.

For each field you flag, return its `where` exactly as given, one of `unknown word` or `lost precision`, and one short line naming the word or the missing specific.

fields.text: A file that version history deliberately ignores is never handed back to the browser.
A local settings file holding passwords is kept out of version history, and would otherwise be readable in the map.
Code shown beside the map is the version the map was built from, not whatever sits on disk now.
A reader comparing a box against edited code would blame the map for a mismatch the map never made.
A version name arriving in a web address is refused unless it reads as an ordinary commit name.
A crafted name could otherwise be taken as an instruction and make the history reader do something else.
Code fetched from the public internet runs in the viewer only when its fingerprint matches the expected one.
A tampered drawing or highlighting library would run inside a page that already shows every line of the project's source.
A source link may open only through an address belonging to a known code editor.
A hand-typed link pattern could otherwise run script in the page or send the reader somewhere unexpected.
Data the product writes only to read back crosses no interface, unless the map records an outside reader.
The map draws the product's own database as an outside edge, so where the product ends disappears.
A step names the service on the far side, never the proxy or the library that carries the call.
The map names the log shipper and never the log store, so the reader cannot tell who receives the data.
Each outside system names the interfaces it stands on, or records why it is none, never both.
A deliberate exclusion looks exactly like nobody having looked, so the whole edge of the product stops being trustworthy.
An interface is labelled by what it is, never by what it is for.
A payment service and a crash reporter get labels nobody can compare, so the picture stops grouping the edge.
Who stands on the far side of an interface is read from the flows, never written by hand.
A hand-written far side disagrees with the stories, and the reader gets two answers with no way to choose.
A person meets the product through an interface at every step, not only the first and the last.
The picture shows one person on both sides of one wall, so the edge of the product reads as optional.
Work the product schedules for itself is never an outsider, so it crosses no interface.
The map counts its own timer as a customer, so an interface handing data to nobody looks answered.
A command is a way in only when it acts on the running product or its stored data.
A build or test command counted as a way in makes the outside edge look wider than it is.
A command judged not to be a way in must still be recorded as a run or build command.
A command decided against and never rewritten disappears from the map. No check can see a row nobody wrote.
A way in is recorded once, at the thing that does the acting, and never again at whatever calls it.
Counting a wrapper and the command it wraps as two doors inflates the outside edge with duplicate rows.
A timer, a boot hook or a queue reader is work the product does to itself, not a way in.
Placing the product's own scheduled work on the outside edge makes it look reachable where nobody outside can reach it.
A way in of a kind nobody recognises is treated as one somebody outside asks for.
Guessing self-started instead would quietly drop a real door out of every count of the outside edge.
Every way in that somebody outside asks for belongs to exactly one interface, or its absence is recorded.
A way in claimed twice, or by nothing, breaks any honest count of where the product meets the world.
Work every request passes through on its way in is not itself a way in, so it joins no interface.
Demanding an interface for shared request handling raises a complaint nobody can ever clear, so readers stop reading complaints.
A way in that no story reaches is reported, including the ones the product starts for itself.
Exempting scheduled work hides a whole background behaviour, with no signal anywhere that it is missing.
